title: Looking from above: bird's-eye view
keyIdea: The same thing can look different from different places. From the side, a party hat (a cone) looks like a triangle and a tin (a cylinder) looks like a rectangle. From above, as a bird sees it, both look like circles: the hat is a circle with a dot in the middle for its point. A box looks like a rectangle from above. A ball looks like a circle from every side, and a block (a cube) is a square from the side and from the top. The thing itself does not change; only the place you look from changes. A plan, or bird's-eye view, shows a room or a playground as it looks from above.
familyTip: Stand over a few things on the floor together: a cup, a ball, a box and a cone such as a party hat or a traffic cone. Say what shape each one looks like from up high. Then lie down flat on the floor and look at them from the side. Which ones changed shape, and which looked the same?

visual.caption: From above, is it round, or does it have corners? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: match toys to their view from above, move the eye, sort same or different, say who saw it, read a plan.

kid: A bird flies high up. It looks down. It sees the top of things. We call this a bird's-eye view.
A party hat looks like a triangle from the side. Look down on it from the top. Now it is a circle, with a dot in the middle. The dot is the point of the hat.
A tin looks like a rectangle from the side. From the top it is a circle. A ball is a circle from the top and from the side. The toy does not change. Only where you look from changes.
A plan is a picture from the top. On a plan, a round sandpit is a circle and a slide is a long, thin rectangle. A box is a rectangle too.
adult: Ages 4 to 5. This is spatial reasoning in DfE Development Matters (2021), Reception Mathematics. Children turn and move shapes to build spatial reasoning, and talk about routes and places. It leads on to KS1 Geography (National Curriculum 2013), where children use aerial photos and plan views and draw a simple map. Key words: view, from above, from the side, bird's-eye view (top view or plan view), plan, circle, square, rectangle, triangle.

Here is how common solids look. A sphere is a circle from every side. A cube is a square from the top and from each side. A cylinder standing on its end is a circle from above and a rectangle from the side. A cone standing on its base is a circle from above, with its point in the middle, and a triangle from the side. A square-based pyramid is a square with lines to the middle from above, and a triangle from the side. A box lying flat is a rectangle from above.

Taking another viewpoint is hard for young children. Piaget and Inhelder (1956) found that young children often pick their own view when asked what someone else sees, and Frick, Möhring and Newcombe (2014) showed that perspective-taking improves a great deal between ages 4 and 8. Real objects help most: let your child look down on a thing, then crouch to see it from the side, and say what changed.

Common mistakes: giving the side view for the top (a party hat looks like a triangle from above), thinking the thing itself changed shape, and thinking everything looks different from above. A ball and a cube do not. In the lab your child matches 4 toys to their top views and moves an eye from the side to the top of 3 toys. They sort 5 toys by whether they look the same both ways, say whether a bird or a child saw 5 pictures, and find 3 things on a plan of a playground.

practice.prompt: A party hat stands on a table. What does it look like from above?
practice.hint: From above you see the round bottom of the hat and its point in the middle.
practice.explain: From above, a party hat is a circle with a dot in the middle. It only looks like a triangle from the side.

practice.prompt: Which toy looks like a circle from every side?
practice.hint: Think of a toy that is round all over.
practice.explain: A ball is round all over, so it is a circle from the top and from the side. A tin is a rectangle from the side.

practice.prompt: A bird looks down on a table. It sees {a} round tins and {b} square blocks. How many things does it see?
practice.hint: Count the tins, then count on the blocks.
practice.explain: {a} tins and {b} blocks make {=a+b} things. From above, the tins look like circles and the blocks look like squares.

practice.prompt: On a plan of the park there are {a} round tree tops. A bird flies over {b} more trees. How many tree tops has the bird seen now?
practice.hint: Start at {a} and count on {b} more.
practice.explain: {a} and {b} more make {=a+b}. From above, each tree is a green circle of leaves.

practice.prompt: You look at a tin from the side. What shape do you see?
practice.hint: From the side you see the tall body of the tin, not its round top.
practice.explain: From the side, a tin looks like a rectangle. From above, you see its round top: a circle.

pool.prompt: A tin of beans stands up. What does it look like from above?
pool.hint: From above you only see the top of the tin.
pool.explain: The top of a tin is round, so from above it is a circle. It is a rectangle from the side.

pool.prompt: A bird flies over a box. What does the bird see?
pool.hint: The top of a box has four straight sides.
pool.explain: The top of a box is a rectangle, so that is what the bird sees from above.

pool.prompt: You look down at a hat, then crouch down to look from the side. Did the hat change shape?
choices: No, only where I look from changed
pool.explain: The hat stayed the same. It looks different because you looked from a different place.

pool.prompt: Which toy looks the same from the side and from the top?
pool.hint: Think of a toy that has a square on every side.
pool.explain: A cube has a square face on every side, so it is a square from the top and from the side.

pool.prompt: On a plan of the park, what shape is the round pond?
pool.hint: A plan shows things as a bird sees them from above.
pool.explain: A plan shows things from above, so a round pond is drawn as a circle.

pool.prompt: From above, a bird sees {a} party hats. Each hat looks like a circle. How many circles does it see?
pool.hint: Each hat makes one circle from above.
pool.explain: One hat makes one circle from above, so {a} hats make {a} circles.

pool.prompt: A pyramid from above looks like ...
choices: A square with lines to the middle
pool.hint: The bottom of this pyramid is a square, and its point is in the middle.
pool.explain: From above you see the square bottom, with lines going up to the point in the middle. It is a triangle from the side.

pool.prompt: You put {a} balls on the floor and look at them from above, then from the side. How many circles do you see from the side?
pool.hint: A ball is a circle from every side.
pool.explain: A ball is a circle from the top and from the side, so {a} balls still make {a} circles.

pool.prompt: Who sees a party hat as a triangle?
pool.hint: Where do you need to be to see the point stick up?
pool.explain: From the side you see the hat's slope up to its point: a triangle. The bird above sees a circle with a dot.
